review.title: Complete thyroid-location assessment

cues.phrase: the lower anterior neck is outside the recorded field
cues.why: The named omission points directly to the only option explicitly completing the missing anatomical coverage.

cues.phrase: Neck ultrasound including the thyroid bed
cues.why: Only this imaging option adds an explicit target/completeness qualifier; CT and MRI are generic modality labels.
A negatively framed omission competes with three investigations after the exhibit stresses missing coverage.

fairness: Completing neck/thyroid ultrasound is a defensible best answer; an unexamined thyroid bed is not evidence of an absent thyroid. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The task is complete and the subsequent infection episode is a coherent separate decision; the first explanation does not name the later timing answer.

Report-wide scope: editorial review of the 20 after/candidate nodes only. The one kept record, 18 retirement/replacement proposals and six held/parked planning records are noted but not scored. No external source verification, runtime audit or clinical approval is conferred. Difficulty and high-yield labels are qualitative judgments, not exam-frequency measurements.
suggestions: Retain the acquisition boundaries, but make every imaging choice comparably explicit about its target and protocol.
Require a consequential distinction between completing an unexamined region and investigating a genuinely examined but unresolved finding; the present missing-region repair is essentially one step.
Do not add an unsupported radionuclide-imaging rule to manufacture difficulty.

review.title: Sequence cyst surgery around infection
clarityIssues: The exhibit repeats the current tenderness, erythema and drainage without adding an independent observation.

cues.phrase: Treatment of the infection is being arranged.
cues.why: Prelabels the current management phase immediately before choosing whether elective surgery waits.
An implausible cancellation endpoint makes the recurrent-symptom history select the only sustained treatment plan.

fairness: Treating the active infection before elective definitive surgery is a defensible best answer. No airway/swallowing warning is supplied that would require a different emergency decision.
Normal thyroid documentation and the later inflammatory episode follow coherently from node 1, and this update supplies the necessary information independently.
The recurrent episodes plus active infection technically affect timing and eventual treatment, but the offered alternatives reduce the decision to a familiar defer-elective-surgery rule.
suggestions: Remove the duplicate current-phase row and the pre-answer management announcement.
Replace cancellation with a credible competing operative strategy or sequence, using supported findings that actually distinguish it.
Keep the distinction between infection treatment and definitive tract treatment; do not make the key imply that urgent drainage is never indicated.

review.title: Assess an incomplete brace trial
clarityIssues: The stem calls this apparent failure before the resident evaluates the treatment exposure. The father remaining in the room adds no treatment discriminator.

cues.why: Signals that the claimed failure should be rejected.

cues.phrase: it rubbed after a growth spurt
cues.why: Nearly states the refitting rationale; the key is already favored without the exhibit.
Directly removes the observation option.

cues.phrase: Arrange Ravitch assessment after unsuccessful bracing
cues.why: The option asserts unsuccessful treatment although the stem emphasizes an interrupted trial, advertising the intended error.

fairness: Orthotic reassessment is reasonable for an intermittently worn, irritating brace with a still-compressible deformity and intact skin.
An assessment for surgery is not equivalent to committing to surgery; it is not categorically inappropriate if a patient cannot tolerate bracing. The current wording overstates the contrast.
Pectus bracing is relevant, but this particular refitting decision is less central to general-surgery board preparation than the main deformity/treatment principles.
suggestions: Use a neutral task and compare concrete next treatment plans at the same commitment level.
Make actual exposure and mechanical response necessary to distinguish a credible competing plan; do not repeat the refitting rationale in the presentation.
Clarify willingness to retry a tolerable brace only if it is necessary for ranking; do not use a preference as a substitute for the clinical inference.

review.title: Act on nonrepresentative node sampling
fairness: The sample contains no lymphoid tissue, so reassurance about the target node is unsupported. Progressive enlargement and fixation then justify representative biopsy rather than surveillance.

Excisional biopsy is a defensible best answer for this concerning pediatric node; repeat FNA is a credible error based on repairing the original sampling miss, but may again fail to provide the architecture needed for diagnosis.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. This does not diagnose lymphoma, and the explanation appropriately avoids doing so.
Standalone task, patient, target and chronology are clear; there is no prior-answer scaffold.
suggestions: Retain both the specimen composition and the progressive fixed examination; they support two distinct consequential inferences.
The explanation could briefly state why an excisional specimen is favored over another FNA here, without claiming FNA is never useful.

review.title: Interpret the site of a reassuring node study
clarityIssues: Routine ENT follow-up has no defined urgency. The choice set changes both specialty and urgency, so it can be read as testing which specialty owns the node.

cues.why: The task repeats a concerning finding that selects prompt assessment even if the entire ultrasound exhibit is removed.
The key is the only expedited escalation beside routine follow-up and surveillance.
The right-versus-left mismatch is easy to spot, but it does not change the already-obvious disposition.

fairness: Prompt specialist assessment is appropriate; the benign appearance of a different node does not reassure about the growing supraclavicular target.
ENT can also assess concerning cervical nodes. The item should not teach a categorical pediatric-surgery-over-ENT distinction without a service-specific reason.
The transition to the mediastinal case is coherent, but this node is not an independent two-step test: the same disposition follows before the report is interpreted.
suggestions: Compare concrete plans at comparable urgency, with the target mismatch determining which workup or tissue route is appropriate.
Use the same specialist destination across urgency alternatives if urgency is the intended objective.
Do not remove the concerning target findings merely to make the ultrasound discrepancy harder.

review.title: Choose a safer tissue route with mediastinal compression
fairness: Orthopnea and CT-demonstrated tracheal narrowing must be interpreted as anesthesia-related risk, then combined with an accessible peripheral tissue target to choose a diagnostic route.
Local-anesthetic peripheral-node excision is a defensible best answer among these plans; both mediastinal alternatives introduce sedation/anesthesia risk in the supplied circumstances.

Prior cooperation and target accessibility are legitimate feasibility data rather than an authored assertion that the keyed plan is safe. Cooperation with a needle procedure does not guarantee tolerance of excision; the real hospital team must assess this.
The later record supplies its own target, symptoms and imaging. The earlier referral explanation does not reveal the biopsy/anesthesia answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the positional symptoms and accessible peripheral target.
Keep this framed as specialist procedural planning, not a guarantee that local anesthesia eliminates all risk.
Optional tightening: replace repeated clinic-versus-hospital framing with one concise record-review sentence.

review.title: Select exertional physiology testing
clarityIssues: The skeletal appearance being unchanged contributes little to the offered test comparison.

cues.why: Directly matches the only exercise-based option.
Explicit adequacy makes the repeat-echo distractor disposable.

cues.phrase: Adequate spirometry is normal, with no bronchodilator response.
cues.why: Explicitly completes the other distractor, leaving only the novel test.
Both distractors repeat completed resting tests; the key is the only new comparison.

fairness: CPET is a reasonable next functional study; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
Normal resting spirometry does not exclude every exercise-related airway disorder. The explanation should not imply it does.
The specific CPET-versus-repeat-resting-test choice is supporting specialty assessment rather than a particularly high-yield general-surgery board discriminator.
Standalone context is adequate, but selecting the only novel exercise test is not two consequential steps.
suggestions: Use equally novel, plausible investigations and observations that distinguish the competing mechanisms of exercise limitation.
Keep actual test adequacy when needed for fairness, while avoiding two deliberately redundant repeat-test foils.
Remove the unchanged skeletal comparison unless it changes the requested decision.

review.title: Act on a concerning examination despite flow

cues.phrase: The report does not explain the abnormal lie or the continuing focal pain.
cues.why: An editorial prompt to distrust the Doppler result. It is unnecessary, though the underlying raw findings still support the answer without it.

fairness: Abrupt pain, vomiting and an abnormal testicular lie sustain concern for torsion despite detected arterial flow. Interpreting the limit of the imaging finding and acting on the clinical risk are consequential steps.
Urgent surgical assessment is the defensible best answer over delaying that assessment for repeat imaging or observation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The retrospective task is clear. The later alternative operative diagnosis does not invalidate the earlier decision to explore, and it is not disclosed in advance.
suggestions: Optional cue cleanup: end the Doppler report after the observed arterial signals; let the resident resolve the discordance.
Preserve the raw urgency findings and avoid adding a management threshold or time cutoff.

review.title: Tailor fixation to operative findings
clarityIssues: The explanation says this consensus without naming a consensus in the visible explanation; use direct teaching wording or an identifiable reference.

cues.phrase: It accounts for the focal tenderness.
cues.why: Supplies the causal interpretation of the appendage finding, but does not resolve the separate attachment-dependent fixation decision.

fairness: The record supplies an alternative cause, an untwisted viable testis and normal attachments without a bell-clapper deformity. Together these support closure without routine fixation in this negative-torsion exploration.

Distinguishing appendage torsion from testicular torsion and using the attachment findings to decide fixation is a meaningful operative application. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; exact consensus applicability remains for clinical sign-off.

The sequence is coherent: a concerning preoperative examination can lead to exploration that identifies another cause. The current operative update stands alone, and prior feedback does not teach the fixation answer.
suggestions: Retain the explicit attachment findings; absence of a cord twist by itself would not establish the same fixation plan.
Optional tightening: report the twisted appendage without announcing that it accounts for the tenderness.
Name or remove the vague consensus reference.

review.title: Investigate recurrent thyroid-region infection

cues.why: A medically meaningful clue to a pharyngeal connection, not a direct wording match to an answer. Retain it.
A weaker repeat-test distractor, but the remaining thyroid-function alternative still requires understanding the recurrent infection pattern.

fairness: Repeated left thyroid-region infection with oropharyngeal organisms supports investigating a congenital pharyngeal tract; choosing a contrast swallow after the acute episode settles follows that inference.
The key is defensible among the offered tests. It should not be taught as the uniquely required investigation over all endoscopic or cross-sectional approaches, which are not compared here.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation appropriately avoids asserting an exact third-versus-fourth classification. The standalone task supplies location, recurrence and phase.
suggestions: Retain the resolved inflammatory phase and infection location.
If strengthening the item, replace the repeat-ultrasound foil with an equally plausible investigation, only after confirming a patient-specific reason that ranks the alternatives.

review.title: Map a recurrent parotid-region tract
clarityIssues: Repeat needle sampling presumes an earlier needle sample, but the visible history establishes local abscess treatments rather than a specific needle-sampling procedure.

cues.phrase: its deeper margin cannot be followed through the parotid region
cues.why: Names the missing extent and the exact region present in the key.

cues.phrase: MRI of the parotid and neck
cues.why: The only new study covering deep anatomy; both distractors repeat local work.

cues.phrase: Repeat ultrasound of the skin opening
cues.why: Artificially restricts the competing ultrasound to the already demonstrated superficial component.

fairness: MRI is a reasonable mapping study for this stable unresolved deep tract. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The item does not meaningfully discriminate MRI from another credible mapping strategy; it mainly compares deeper assessment with deliberately repeated superficial work.
The basic branchial anomaly is testable, but this exact modality comparison is relatively specialized and less high-yield.
The later operative case is coherent; however, this explanation already tells the resident to define the deeper parotid course before another local operation.
suggestions: Use same-stage mapping alternatives with a supported reason to choose one; do not merely replace ultrasound with CT unless the vignette can fairly rank them.
Remove repeat from needle sampling unless a prior needle sample is actually documented.
Limit feedback to why the investigation is appropriate so that the companion retains a distinct operative inference.

review.title: Plan complete tract excision around parotid anatomy

cues.why: Directly maps to through a parotid approach in the key.

cues.phrase: Earlier procedures drained or removed the visible superficial component; drainage recurred.
cues.why: Explicitly discredits the skin-confined option.
An excessive extreme frames the key as the obvious middle choice.

cues.phrase: define the deeper course through the parotid region
cues.why: The preceding node explanation rehearses the depth and location that select the keyed exposure.

fairness: A parotid approach for complete first-branchial tract excision with facial-nerve preservation is defensible; routine total gland removal is not justified by this record.
The later update stands alone and the timeline is coherent, but the new map does not produce much reasoning after the previous explanation.

The named operation does not expressly include facial-nerve identification. That safety concept appears only indirectly in the explanation and is the more important surgical learning point. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Make the new anatomy change a real operative plan rather than simply matching the word parotid.
Use credible competing exposures or nerve-management plans and state only supported anatomy needed to distinguish them.
Address facial-nerve identification/preservation concretely in the post-answer teaching, and remove prior-feedback rehearsal.

review.title: Distinguish mycobacterial node surgery from abscess drainage

cues.why: Only the key carries the specialist qualifier, giving it a modest authority cue; the clinical distinction remains meaningful without that word.

fairness: The indolent painless course, violet thinning skin and lack of response to routine antibacterial treatment support a mycobacterial process rather than an ordinary acute pyogenic abscess. That distinction changes excision versus drainage.
Excision is a defensible best local surgical plan among these choices; the explanation appropriately states that no pathogen is proven and that nerve/anatomical risk matters.

This does not establish that excision is mandatory for every suspected mycobacterial node or superior to all nonsurgical pathways in every location. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified within the question's local-surgery scope.
The standalone task is complete; no prior feedback supplies the answer.
suggestions: Optional cue cleanup: put specialist planning in the shared task or remove specialist from the key alone.
Retain the anatomical-risk limitation; a later version comparing surgery with nonsurgical treatment would need enough site/risk information to rank them.

review.title: Escalate persistent suppuration after medical treatment
clarityIssues: The exhibit repeats the discordant clinical response already stated in the update; the ultrasound adds the new information.
fairness: Improved fever does not establish source control when the local swelling becomes larger, tender and fluctuant and ultrasound shows a collection. Interpreting divergent responses then escalating toward drainage is a consequential two-step decision.

Surgical drainage assessment is the defensible best answer over unchanged observation or elective whole-node excision. The key does not assert that an operation has already been performed or specify an unsupported timing threshold.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The retrospective framing is clear and the standalone record supplies the response and focal findings.
suggestions: Optional tightening: state the systemic/local response once and keep the ultrasound observation.
Keep the key at assessment/planning scope unless adding sufficient supported detail to select a particular drainage procedure.

review.title: Do not infer absence from a negative localization scan
clarityIssues: The repeated nonpalpability and negative-ultrasound details occur in both presentation/update and exhibit.

cues.phrase: Specialist examination under anesthesia and exploration
cues.why: The sole definitive specialist plan is contrasted with two imaging detours.
Repeats a study already reported as not visualizing the gonad, making this a weak foil.
Both distractors share this delaying qualifier, while only the key proceeds to the common endpoint.

fairness: A negative localization ultrasound does not establish absence. Specialist examination under anesthesia followed by appropriately tailored exploration is a defensible best answer.
The governing rule is high-yield, but the current choice set tests it directly rather than requiring two consequential inferences.
The operative companion follows coherently and is not explicitly answered by this explanation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Remove duplicate data and make the next-step decision depend on a meaningful examination or prior-workup distinction.
Compare credible plans at the same stage rather than exploration against two imaging delays.
If kept as foundational recognition, obtain an explicit basic-item exception; do not count it as a difficult resident item.

review.title: Follow the operative vascular/vas route

cues.why: The anatomy term overlaps with the only option following that named route.

cues.phrase: the vessels are not seen ending blindly within the abdomen
cues.why: Provides the explicit converse of the rule and pre-eliminates stopping.

cues.phrase: Complete the operation without groin exploration
cues.why: Describes the distractor as omission of the keyed procedure rather than a neutral operative endpoint.

fairness: Vas and vessels entering the internal ring with no intra-abdominal testis support inguinal exploration; the supplied findings do not establish testicular absence.
This is useful operative anatomy, but following a named route is a single familiar rule in the present option set. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The update is independently complete and follows the preceding exploration plan. Prior feedback does not reveal the inguinal answer.
suggestions: Retain the observed vas/vessel course, but remove redundant converse teaching if it contributes no independent finding.
Use neutral, credible operative alternatives instead of a without-groin-exploration label.
Create a supported anatomical distinction that changes the next action, or explicitly retain this as basic anatomy rather than claim hard two-step reasoning.

review.title: Recognize the need for chromosomal assessment
clarityIssues: Which investigation should be included is not a single-best-next-step task: a DSD evaluation may include chromosomal and anatomical investigations. The intended ordering or diagnostic question is unspecified.
Recorded as male since birth is unnecessarily repeated with boy when the actual decision-critical information is the genital and gonadal examination.

cues.why: Flags uncertainty about sex development before the anatomical evidence is interpreted.
The only nonlocalization test among two imaging alternatives; it is easy to select by recognizing the conventional phenotype-to-workup association.

fairness: The combination of proximal hypospadias and bilateral nonpalpable gonads supports DSD/endocrine assessment including chromosomal analysis.

Uncertainty: pelvic MRI is not necessarily the preferred initial anatomical study, but anatomical imaging can be part of a DSD evaluation. The broad included wording does not establish that it is categorically inappropriate. This is a task-ranking ambiguity, not a claim that MRI is required.
The explanation should not imply chromosomal testing alone constitutes the full indicated assessment. It does mention endocrine/DSD review, which is appropriate.
The concept is high-yield, but the current task is a direct syndrome-to-investigation association, not two consequential steps.
suggestions: Ask one specific next decision before routine repair and give comparable investigation or referral plans that can actually be ranked.
State relevant already-completed assessment only when necessary to resolve the closest alternative; do not name chromosomal uncertainty in the task as a cue.
Keep phenotype, sex recorded at birth and gender identity conceptually distinct; avoid treating any one as proof of the others.

review.title: Map vessels before congenital lung surgery
clarityIssues: The acquisition row restates noncontrast CT with multiple additional descriptions of absent contrast.

cues.phrase: there is no arterial or venous contrast acquisition in its protocol
cues.why: Names exactly the missing acquisition that the keyed contrast test supplies.
Only contrast option against two explicitly Noncontrast options; knowledge of the actual congenital lesion is barely needed.

fairness: Preoperative vascular mapping is reasonable for a persistent congenital-appearing lung lesion because cystic appearance does not exclude a systemic arterial component. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The clinical concept is high-yield, but the exhibit and options turn it into a missing-contrast completion task rather than interpretation followed by a surgical decision.
The standalone task is clear, and documenting acquisition rather than merely missing exported images is sound.
suggestions: State the acquisition once and use comparably credible imaging protocols.
Make a raw lesion or vascular finding determine a consequential preoperative decision; do not tell the resident the vascular conclusion in the caption.
Do not introduce an equally appropriate angiographic alternative without supplying a supported reason to rank it.

review.title: Sequence diaphragmatic repair with physiology

cues.why: The respiratory trajectory explicitly contrasts worsening with recovery, making stabilization the obvious safe option.
The only option addressing instability is contrasted with two immediate operations.
Shares immediate repair with the thoracoscopic distractor, reducing the apparent three-way comparison to one timing rule.

fairness: Escalating respiratory and vasoactive support with falling urine output supports continued stabilization rather than routine immediate repair. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The two surgical options differ in approach despite a timing task; that difference cannot rescue the unsupported immediate-repair timing.
This is an important high-yield CDH principle, but multiple abnormal findings do not create a second consequential inference when all point to the same familiar stabilize-first rule.
The outside ICU record makes the clinical setting and chronology clear.
suggestions: Compare distinct credible timing plans under a genuinely interpretable physiologic trajectory rather than open versus thoracoscopic versions of the same premature operation.
Use only verified readiness criteria if a more nuanced timing decision requires them; do not invent cutoffs.
Alternatively retain the item as an explicitly accepted foundational CDH safety item, with easy difficulty and no two-step claim.

review.title: Evaluate a repaired diaphragm when symptoms change
clarityIssues: The current examination and chronology are repeated in the exhibit rather than adding decision-changing information.

cues.phrase: new combined chest and upper-abdominal findings
cues.why: The task highlights the intended unifying anatomical interpretation.

cues.phrase: intermittent gurgling in that region after eating
cues.why: A strong classic clue; clinically legitimate, but paired with the only basic structural chest study it makes the decision straightforward.
The only direct broad structural study beside airway physiology and cardiac assessment.

fairness: Chest radiographs are a defensible initial study for a stable child with prior CDH repair and new meal-related thoracoabdominal findings. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The history and examination imply a structural concern, but choosing a chest film against physiologic/cardiac tests is a simple recognition-to-test association rather than two substantial inferences.
The standalone case is coherent, and the explanation appropriately keeps recurrence provisional rather than proven.
suggestions: Delete duplicate chronology/examination rows and use a neutral complete task.
For resident difficulty, supply a meaningful new investigation result or competing explanation that changes the subsequent action, using credible same-stage alternatives.
Keep the stable status and warning-feature distinction; do not manufacture difficulty by omitting acute obstructive or respiratory findings.

sourceCase.displayName: Discuss brace assessment for pectus carinatum
sourceCase.presentation: Chloe Harris, a 16-year-old girl, visits the clinic with her father, Michael Harris, who remains in the same room throughout the visit. Chloe has a stable outward anterior chest-wall prominence diagnosed as pectus carinatum. She has no chest pain or breathlessness and would like to consider active nonsurgical care. She and her father ask whether a chest brace could be suitable; she is willing to discuss the practical commitment.

His father wonders whether the chest shape proves why Samuel cannot keep up with teammates.

nodes.objective: Interpret the coverage of a prior neck study and select an adequate ultrasound assessment before cyst excision.
nodes.currentUpdate: An outside ultrasound report and its acquisition log are reviewed before a surgical referral.

items.label: Acquisition boundaries
items.value: Images extend from the tongue base to the hyoid; the lower anterior neck is outside the recorded field.

items.label: Visible lesion
items.value: A fluid-filled structure is present near the hyoid. There is no current tenderness or skin inflammation.

nodes.task: What is the next imaging plan for Sofia Alvarez's preoperative neck evaluation?

choices.label: Neck ultrasound including the thyroid bed
choices.rationale: The earlier acquisition does not establish thyroid location; complete the ultrasound assessment before considering excision.
choices.temptation: Resolves a specific coverage gap with the usual first imaging method.
choices.residentError: None in this defined acquisition.
choices.decidingObservation: The lower neck lay outside the acquired field.
choices.counterfactual: With a complete study documenting normal thyroid tissue, further imaging might be unnecessary.

choices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck
choices.rationale: CT can characterize complex neck disease, but the outstanding question here can be addressed by completing ultrasound.
choices.temptation: Treat a prior ultrasound as a failed modality rather than a limited acquisition.
choices.residentError: Escalating modality before interpreting what was actually scanned.
choices.decidingObservation: The lesion was seen; the required lower-neck coverage was absent.
choices.counterfactual: Deep extension or a complicated lesion not characterized by ultrasound could justify CT.

choices.label: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the neck
choices.rationale: MRI is not required to answer the routine thyroid-location question in this otherwise localized presentation.
choices.temptation: Prefer a detailed study after seeing any incomplete report.
choices.residentError: Confusing greater imaging complexity with the missing information.
choices.decidingObservation: No deep or extensive process is described.
choices.counterfactual: An unresolved deep congenital tract after ultrasound could require MRI.

choices.label: Proceed without further neck imaging
choices.rationale: The cyst image does not establish whether normal thyroid tissue is present in its usual location.
choices.temptation: Accept the reported cyst as a complete preoperative assessment.
choices.residentError: Equating a represented lesion with a represented thyroid bed.
choices.decidingObservation: The acquisition boundaries exclude the lower neck.
choices.counterfactual: A complete adequate ultrasound with a documented orthotopic thyroid would support this choice.

nodes.explanation: The prior scan characterized the lump but did not cover the lower thyroid bed. Complete neck/thyroid ultrasound before proceeding toward excision. A missing acquisition region is different from a negative examination of that region.
reasoningSteps: Read the acquisition boundaries to determine that thyroid location was not assessed.
Choose an ultrasound that supplies the missing preoperative information rather than treating the cyst image as surgical clearance.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Proceed without further imaging because the cyst already appears localized.
nodes.decidingObservation: The acquisition stops at the hyoid rather than surveying the lower thyroid bed.
nodes.counterfactual: If the same record covered the thyroid bed and documented a normal gland, choose no further imaging from these options.
nodes.deletionTest: Deleting acquisition boundaries leaves the reader unable to distinguish an adequate prior study from an incomplete one; retain them. Removed a sentence explicitly saying thyroid imaging was still needed.

authorGate.cueAttack: The task asks for a plan, allowing the no-imaging option. No stem says to repeat ultrasound; field boundaries replace that named omission. All three tests have waits.
authorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: Four preoperative imaging plans, including a justified no-further-imaging competitor.
authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Coverage interpretation changes whether another study is needed and which study fits that gap.
authorGate.predictedDifficulty: Moderate: the closest error is accepting the outside report without reviewing the acquired region.
authorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: The incomplete lower-neck acquisition favors ultrasound; changing it to a complete normal assessment makes no further imaging appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceCheck: Initial feedback does not teach the later active-infection timing decision. The later result is not shown at this node.

nodes.objective: Use current inflammatory findings to choose the timing of an otherwise indicated thyroglossal cyst operation.
nodes.currentUpdate: Subsequent ultrasound documents a midline cyst and a normal thyroid gland. At a later clinic review, Sofia has a tender red swelling with new purulent drainage. She has no breathing or swallowing difficulty. Treatment of the infection is being arranged.

items.label: Earlier course
items.value: Several episodes of swelling and drainage have interrupted normal activity.

items.label: Current phase
items.value: Tenderness, erythema and purulent drainage are present today.

nodes.task: Which operative plan fits Sofia Alvarez's current neck-cyst episode?

choices.label: Schedule Sistrunk after infection resolution
choices.rationale: Treat the active infection before elective definitive cyst/tract surgery.
choices.temptation: Uses the current disease phase rather than the recurrent-cyst label.
choices.residentError: None in this phase.
choices.decidingObservation: Purulent drainage and inflammation are present now.
choices.counterfactual: A quiescent symptomatic cyst with a normal thyroid could proceed to elective operative assessment.

choices.label: Proceed with Sistrunk during this episode
choices.rationale: Recurrent symptoms support definitive treatment, but active infection changes its timing.
choices.temptation: Apply a source-control impulse to every recurrent draining lesion.
choices.residentError: Treating definitive congenital-tract excision as the first step during active infection.
choices.decidingObservation: The record describes current inflammatory drainage, not a healed previous episode.
choices.counterfactual: After infection has resolved, elective Sistrunk planning becomes appropriate.

choices.label: Cancel Sistrunk after infection resolution
choices.rationale: Resolution of one infection does not remove the recurrent symptomatic tract problem.
choices.temptation: Mistake response of infection for permanent cure of the congenital lesion.
choices.residentError: Conflating temporary inflammatory resolution with definitive tract treatment.
choices.decidingObservation: The recurrent symptomatic course predates today's infection.
choices.counterfactual: If specialist reassessment established a different transient lesion rather than a persistent thyroglossal cyst, this operation would no longer fit.

nodes.explanation: Today's inflammatory episode should be treated before elective Sistrunk surgery. A history of recurrent symptoms still supports definitive specialist planning once the infection settles; improvement of an infection does not itself remove the tract.
reasoningSteps: Distinguish current active infection from the earlier noninflamed cyst assessment.
Retain the definitive operation but move it to the post-infection phase.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Operate now because repeated drainage is read as an immediate definitive-source-control indication.
nodes.decidingObservation: There is active tenderness, erythema and purulent drainage at this review.
nodes.counterfactual: With resolved inflammation and persistent symptomatic cyst, the defer-for-active-infection decision no longer applies and elective surgery can proceed.
nodes.deletionTest: Removing today's update converts the task to Sistrunk recall. Kept current inflammatory findings and removed routine operative anatomy from the task.

authorGate.cueAttack: All choices name the same operation and vary timing policy. The task does not announce that surgery must wait; no option includes its own rationale.
authorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: Three operative timing policies; infection treatment is shared background care.
authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Infer the active phase from the new findings, then distinguish temporary deferral from abandoning definitive treatment.
authorGate.predictedDifficulty: Moderate prediction from competing source-control and elective-infection sequencing errors; requires independent difficulty review.
authorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: Current infection resolves the timing comparison. Quiescent findings change the operative timing.
authorGate.sequenceCheck: Earlier imaging feedback addresses coverage, not this timing rule. The current update changes the key boundary.

nodes.objective: Distinguish an inadequately tolerated brace course from established failure and select renewed specialist brace assessment.
nodes.currentUpdate: Chloe remains bothered by the chest prominence and wants corrective treatment.

items.label: Actual exposure
items.value: She wore the brace only intermittently before stopping it; rubbing marks faded after she stopped.

items.label: Examination
items.value: Gentle pressure still substantially reduces the prominence. The skin is intact today.

nodes.task: Which treatment plan fits Chloe Harris's apparent bracing failure?

choices.label: Arrange orthotic refitting and supervised bracing
choices.rationale: Flexible anatomy and an interrupted poorly tolerated course support specialist refitting/reassessment before concluding the treatment is ineffective.
choices.temptation: Treats the documented barrier to an adequate trial.
choices.residentError: None in this course.
choices.decidingObservation: The wall remains compressible and actual brace exposure was limited by rubbing.
choices.counterfactual: A well-delivered unsuccessful course with unsuitable stiff anatomy would make operative assessment more reasonable.

choices.label: Arrange Ravitch assessment after unsuccessful bracing
choices.rationale: Operative assessment can be appropriate after unsuitable or unsuccessful bracing, but the present course did not establish that failure.
choices.temptation: Take the patient's label of failure as evidence of an adequate trial.
choices.residentError: Ignoring the dose of actual treatment and the fit problem.
choices.decidingObservation: Intermittent use ended because of rubbing after growth.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent deformity after an adequately tolerated supervised course could justify a surgical discussion.

choices.label: Arrange observation after ending corrective treatment
choices.rationale: Observation remains possible, but Chloe seeks correction and has a remediable barrier to a supported nonsurgical option.
choices.temptation: Treat intolerance as a reason to abandon correction.
choices.residentError: Confusing the previous brace's fit with an unavoidable limit of all bracing.
choices.decidingObservation: Her wall remains flexible and she still seeks active treatment.
choices.counterfactual: A patient who no longer wants correction and has no concerning symptoms could choose observation.

nodes.explanation: An interrupted, poorly fitting brace course does not establish biological treatment failure. Return to the chest-wall/orthotic service to reassess fit and a tolerable supervised plan. Do not prescribe a pressure or guarantee correction from this record.
reasoningSteps: Interpret limited exposure and rubbing as a barrier to a meaningful trial rather than proof of brace resistance.

choices.decidingObservation: New focal basal signs and meal-related abdominal symptoms are not explained by that attribution.
choices.counterfactual: New cardiac or pulmonary-vascular findings in a CDH survivor could make echocardiography appropriate.

nodes.explanation: A repaired diaphragm can later recur; earlier reassuring follow-up does not settle a new symptom pattern. Obtain chest imaging for the new coupled findings and escalate care if acute respiratory or obstructive features develop. This tests symptom-directed evaluation, not a fixed surveillance schedule or a proven recurrence diagnosis.
reasoningSteps: Relate new coupled thoracic/meal findings to the history of diaphragmatic repair rather than accepting an old reassuring assessment.
Choose an initial anatomical study before assigning the symptoms to chronic airway or vascular disease.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Attribute new breathlessness to chronic pulmonary disease without investigating the changed localizing pattern.
nodes.decidingObservation: Meal-related abdominal symptoms occur with new focal left chest findings after repair.
nodes.counterfactual: An isolated wheeze/airflow question with no new focal or meal-related findings could favor spirometry; new vascular/cardiac findings could favor echocardiography.
nodes.deletionTest: The old repair, interval change and coupled localizing findings each affect the study choice. Removed an exact recurrence probability and a universal surveillance interval.

authorGate.cueAttack: The complaint gives symptoms rather than recurrence. All options are named studies with waits. No fictional radiograph is promised and no diagnosis is given by the task.
authorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: Three initial studies for changed symptoms at follow-up.
authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret the changed pattern in a repair survivor, then choose the study that investigates anatomy before attributing a comorbidity.
authorGate.predictedDifficulty: Moderate: avoid an understandable chronic-lung or pulmonary-hypertension attribution after neonatal CDH.
authorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: The coupled focal findings favor chest imaging. A purely airflow or vascular pattern changes the choice. One directly verified follow-up review supports this narrow application.
authorGate.sequenceCheck: Standalone. It is not a continuation of the neonatal timing case and cannot inherit its diagnosis/physiology answer.

cases.presentation: Sofia Alvarez, a 24-year-old woman, attends clinic for a recurrent upper-midline neck lump that rises with tongue movement.

Chloe Harris, a 16-year-old girl, attends clinic with her father, Michael Harris, who remains in the room. She stopped her pectus carinatum brace because it rubbed after a growth spurt and thinks the treatment has failed.

Lucas Ellis, a 14-year-old boy, attends clinic with his mother, Sarah Ellis, who remains in the room. A firm cervical lump continues to enlarge after an outside needle sample was described to the family as reassuring.

Grace Turner, an 11-year-old girl, attends clinic with her father, James Turner, who remains in the room. A lump above her left collarbone has enlarged despite a recent ultrasound report describing a benign-looking neck node.

Samuel Price, a 17-year-old boy, attends clinic with his father, Andrew Price, who remains in the room. He has pectus excavatum and reproducible breathlessness during running, with comfortable breathing at rest.
Ben Archer, a 12-year-old boy, is the named patient in outside hospital records that the founder reviews with his mother, Laura Archer, in clinic after his discharge.

Nora Ward, a 6-year-old girl, attends clinic with her mother, Helen Ward, who remains in the room. The founder reviews outside records of repeated left lower-neck infections involving the upper thyroid region.
Olivia Lane, a 9-year-old girl, attends clinic with her mother, Rachel Lane, who remains in the room. Repeated drainage near the left mandibular angle has persisted after local abscess treatments.
Mina Patel, a 6-year-old girl, attends clinic with her mother, Anita Patel, who remains in the room. She has a persistent unilateral cervical swelling.
Liam Brooks, a 10-year-old boy, is the named patient in outside hospital records that the founder reviews with his father, Paul Brooks, in clinic after discharge.

Oliver Reed, a 12-year-old boy, attends clinic with his father, Mason Reed, who remains in the room. The left testis has not been felt on repeated specialist examinations; an outside localization ultrasound reported no left testis.

Noah Wells, a 5-year-old boy recorded as male since birth, attends clinic with his father, Daniel Wells, who remains in the room. The family brings outside records before a proposed routine genital operation.

Ava Morris, a 6-year-old girl, attends clinic with her mother, Claire Morris, who remains in the room. The founder reviews outside imaging after repeated infections in the same left lower-lung region.
Isla Chen, a 2-day-old girl, is the named patient in outside neonatal ICU records that the founder reviews with her mother, Mei Chen, in clinic. Isla is being treated at that hospital.

Eva Morris, a 9-year-old girl, attends clinic with her mother, Claire Morris, who remains in the room. Outside records document a patch repair of a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia during infancy. She now has breathlessness and upper-abdominal discomfort after meals.

authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret specimen and site records to determine that the reassuring pathology did not sample the tracked mass. Select representative excisional tissue from the progressive target rather than repeating the wrong site or accepting a limited cytological sample.

authorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: Representative excision and FNA limitations are supported by IPSO for progressive accessible nodes. The task does not invalidate all FNA or suggest that ENT cannot assess promptly. Safe access is a required case constraint.

nodes.objective: Interpret the coverage of a prior neck study and select an adequate ultrasound assessment before cyst excision.
nodes.currentUpdate: Sofia brings the outside imaging transfer for review before cyst surgery is planned. There has been no interval change in the lump.

items.label: Received transfer
items.value: Two images show the fluid-filled lesion near the hyoid.

items.label: Acquisition index
items.value: The same examination lists separate right-thyroid, left-thyroid and isthmus series. Those series remain in the originating archive and can be retrieved for review.

nodes.task: Which imaging plan should precede the operative decision for Sofia Alvarez's midline neck cyst?

choices.label: Review the archived neck and thyroid ultrasound series
choices.rationale: The transfer is incomplete, while the index shows that thyroid series were acquired. Review those existing images for adequacy and thyroid location before another study.
choices.temptation: Use existing images without assuming their contents are normal.
choices.residentError: No error if identity, adequacy and thyroid tissue are checked.
choices.decidingObservation: The omitted received images have corresponding acquired series in the archive.
choices.counterfactual: If the acquisition ended at the hyoid with no thyroid series, repeat complete neck/thyroid ultrasound would be appropriate.

choices.label: Repeat ultrasound of the neck cyst and thyroid
choices.rationale: Repeat ultrasound is reasonable if the thyroid region was not acquired or the images are inadequate; the retrievable archived series should first be examined here.
choices.temptation: The received cyst images do not establish thyroid location.
choices.residentError: Treat a transfer omission as a failed acquisition.
choices.decidingObservation: The archive contains the indexed thyroid series.
choices.counterfactual: If these series were never acquired, were irretrievable or proved inadequate, repeat ultrasound would become reasonable.

choices.label: Obtain contrast CT of the neck cyst and thyroid
choices.rationale: No described deep complication requires CT before the existing thyroid ultrasound series have been reviewed.
choices.temptation: An incomplete transfer can tempt a more extensive modality.
choices.residentError: Escalate modality before resolving acquisition versus transfer provenance.
choices.decidingObservation: The lesion is unchanged and thyroid series are retrievable.
choices.counterfactual: An unresolved deep extension or complication after appropriate ultrasound review could justify CT.

nodes.explanation: The received transfer and the acquired examination are different records. The index indicates that thyroid imaging exists, so retrieve and assess it before repeating or escalating the study. Thyroid location still needs confirmation on adequate images; the index alone does not establish normal thyroid tissue.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the acquisition index and transferred contents as evidence of an export omission rather than an unexamined thyroid region.
Review the existing thyroid series for adequacy before choosing repeat ultrasound or a more extensive modality.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Repeat complete ultrasound because the transferred file contains only cyst images.
nodes.decidingObservation: Both thyroid lobes and the isthmus have indexed, retrievable series from the same examination.
nodes.counterfactual: Replace the index with an acquisition ending at the hyoid and no thyroid series in the archive: repeat neck/thyroid ultrasound becomes the best plan among these options.
nodes.deletionTest: Transfer contents and acquisition index each change the decision; removing either prevents the provenance distinction. Interval stability limits an independent reason to repeat the study. No radionuclide or functional-thyroid rule is added.

authorGate.cueAttack: Every choice names an actual imaging plan and its neck/thyroid target. Removed the negative no-imaging foil and uniquely qualified ultrasound. The archive is a raw acquisition fact, not a statement that thyroid tissue is normal.
authorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: Three imaging plans before the operative decision: existing-image review, repeat acquisition or cross-sectional acquisition.
authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret the acquisition index and transferred contents as evidence of an export omission rather than an unexamined thyroid region. Review the existing thyroid series for adequacy before choosing repeat ultrasound or a more extensive modality.

authorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: Original series are explicitly retrievable and the problem is unchanged. The key requires image review rather than clearance from an index. Failed acquisition changes the answer to repeat ultrasound.

nodes.task: Which definitive operative plan best fits Sofia Alvarez's prior procedure and current findings?

choices.label: Sistrunk excision after further infection management
choices.rationale: Local inflammation changes timing, while retained tract and hyoid explain why repeating cyst-only excision is inadequate.
choices.temptation: Reconcile partial infection response with the earlier limited operation.
choices.residentError: No error when acute infection care continues alongside later definitive planning.
choices.decidingObservation: Fever improved but local inflammation persists; the earlier operation left tract and hyoid.
choices.counterfactual: If local inflammation had also resolved, elective Sistrunk planning need not wait for another infection-free interval.

choices.label: Sistrunk excision as the next treatment
choices.rationale: The extent is appropriate, but absence of fever does not establish resolution of active local infection.
choices.temptation: Read systemic improvement as completed infection treatment.
choices.residentError: Use fever resolution instead of the current local disease phase.
choices.decidingObservation: Tenderness, erythema and purulent drainage remain today.
choices.counterfactual: If local inflammation and drainage had resolved, proceeding to elective Sistrunk would become reasonable.

choices.label: Cyst-only excision after further infection management

choices.temptation: Repeat the familiar simple operation after the infection settles.
choices.residentError: Correct timing while leaving the congenital tract problem.
choices.decidingObservation: The record documents retained central hyoid and superior tract with recurrent symptoms.
choices.counterfactual: A specialist-confirmed isolated superficial cyst without a thyroglossal tract would require a different limited excision plan.

nodes.explanation: Improvement in fever is not resolution of the tender, draining local episode. Treat the current infection before elective definitive excision. The earlier cyst-only operation also left the tract-bearing central hyoid region, so the later plan should address the cyst, tract and central hyoid through a Sistrunk procedure. Urgent drainage for a separate abscess or airway problem is a different decision and is not excluded by this elective plan.

Use prior operative extent to retain definitive tract/hyoid surgery while placing it after infection resolution.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Proceed with Sistrunk now because fever resolved and the recurrent lesion needs source control.
nodes.decidingObservation: Tenderness, erythema and purulent drainage persist after systemic improvement.
nodes.counterfactual: If local tenderness, erythema and drainage had resolved while the tract remained, Sistrunk excision as the next treatment becomes the best of these plans; further infection-related deferral is unnecessary.
nodes.deletionTest: Local findings distinguish infection resolution from fever response. Prior extent distinguishes Sistrunk from repeat cyst-only excision. Documented thyroid location prevents an unasked functional-thyroid problem. No duplicate phase row or cancellation endpoint remains.

nodes.explanation: Read the focal and systemic response separately. Lower fever does not resolve an enlarging fluctuant cervical collection after intravenous treatment. Arrange surgical drainage assessment; do not transfer the indolent mycobacterial-node operation to this acute pyogenic presentation.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that systemic improvement and focal progression are discordant responses.
Apply the persistent pyogenic-collection pathway rather than observation or a different organism's operation.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Continue the same medical plan because the fever has improved.
nodes.decidingObservation: The focal collection enlarges and becomes fluctuant while systemic signs improve.
nodes.counterfactual: If focal swelling and tenderness also regressed without a persistent collection, ongoing medical treatment would be reasonable.
nodes.deletionTest: The divergent response is essential; without it, treatment failure is an unsupported label. Removed an exact elapsed treatment duration and an unverified drug regimen.

nodes.currentUpdate: Examination documents a proximal urethral opening and no palpable gonad on either side. Noah is comfortable, eating normally and has no vomiting or dehydration. Multidisciplinary endocrine/urologic assessment is underway.

items.label: Completed laboratory result

nodes.task: Which biochemical study should be prioritized next in Noah Wells's preoperative assessment?

choices.label: Baseline serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone
choices.rationale: The 46,XX result with nonpalpable gonads changes the explanation of the external anatomy. Screen for an adrenal steroid disorder rather than assuming the unseen gonads are testes.
choices.temptation: Connect the completed chromosome result to the biochemical question before surgery.
choices.residentError: No error with specialist interpretation, appropriate assay and follow-up.
choices.decidingObservation: The chromosome result is 46,XX and neither gonad is palpable.
choices.counterfactual: After a borderline baseline 17-hydroxyprogesterone result, a stimulated adrenal profile rather than another initial screen becomes appropriate.

choices.label: Baseline serum anti-Mullerian hormone
choices.rationale: AMH can assess testicular tissue in a different nonpalpable-gonad context; it does not take priority over the adrenal screen raised by this completed 46,XX result.
choices.temptation: Treat every empty scrotum as a testicular presence-or-absence problem.
choices.residentError: Retain an assumed testicular identity after the chromosome result changes the differential.
choices.decidingObservation: This is 46,XX, not an established 46,XY testicular-regression assessment.
choices.counterfactual: With 46,XY bilateral nonpalpable gonads and a question about functioning testicular tissue, AMH could form part of specialist assessment.

choices.label: Cosyntropin-stimulated adrenal steroid profile
choices.rationale: A stimulated full profile helps when the initial screen is borderline or further characterization is needed; the supported initial screen has not been obtained in this stable child past infancy.
choices.temptation: Start with the most extensive adrenal investigation.
choices.residentError: Skip the stated initial screening stage without a borderline result.
choices.decidingObservation: There is no prior steroid screen and the child is clinically stable.
choices.counterfactual: A borderline baseline 17-hydroxyprogesterone result makes a stimulated full adrenal profile the next study.

nodes.explanation: The chromosome result prevents assuming that bilateral nonpalpable gonads are simply undescended testes. An adrenal cause of virilization needs evaluation. For a stable symptomatic child past infancy, the Endocrine Society supports baseline early-morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone by LC-MS/MS as the initial screen; borderline results need further specialist testing. This is one prioritized step within full multidisciplinary assessment, not a complete DSD workup or a decision about gender identity or genital surgery.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the 46,XX result with bilateral nonpalpable gonads and external findings rather than assigning unseen gonads a testicular identity.
Choose initial adrenal biochemical screening, distinguishing it from testicular-function testing and confirmation after a borderline result.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Order a stimulated full adrenal profile immediately because it is more comprehensive than an initial screen.
nodes.decidingObservation: A 46,XX result is complete, but no prior steroid screen exists in a stable child past infancy.
nodes.counterfactual: Replace the absent steroid record with a borderline baseline 17-hydroxyprogesterone result: the cosyntropin-stimulated adrenal profile becomes the next study among these choices.
nodes.deletionTest: The chromosome result changes the differential; no prior steroid test establishes stage; clinical stability prevents an unstated resuscitation problem. Removed sex-record wording and broad included-investigation wording.

authorGate.cueAttack: All alternatives are named biochemical studies, rather than one chromosome test against localization images. The task specifies the initial next step after a completed result, without naming CAH or announcing an adrenal diagnosis.
authorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: Three biochemical investigations in the same preoperative endocrine assessment. Referral/supportive care are shared and no genital operation is selected.
authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret the 46,XX result with bilateral nonpalpable gonads and external findings rather than assigning unseen gonads a testicular identity. authorGate.predictedDifficulty: Moderate author prediction: infer the changed differential, then select initial screening versus credible confirmatory testing. This is not claimed independently hard.

nodes.objective: Interpret a worsening support trajectory in congenital diaphragmatic hernia and choose stabilization before repair.
nodes.currentUpdate: The referring team asks about the repair sequence. She remains intubated on conventional ventilation; the chest radiograph still shows bowel in the left hemithorax.

items.label: Last 24 hours
items.value: FiO2 0.30 with preductal saturation 93-95%; urine output 2 mL/kg/hour; lactate 1.5 mmol/L; blood pressure within the unit's normal range for gestational age without inotropes.

items.label: Echocardiography trend
items.value: Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure fell from 75 to 45 mmHg. Simultaneous systemic systolic pressure is now 70 mmHg; ventricular function is preserved.

nodes.task: Which repair-sequencing plan is best supported by Isla Chen's current outside ICU record?

choices.label: Plan repair while continuing the present ICU support
choices.rationale: Respiratory, perfusion and pressure trajectories support multidisciplinary repair assessment despite residual pulmonary hypertension and intubation.
choices.temptation: Distinguish readiness from complete normalization or removal of support.
choices.residentError: No error when the outside team confirms the full assessment and perioperative plan.
choices.decidingObservation: Adequate perfusion and reduced oxygen support persist; estimated pulmonary pressure is below systemic.
choices.counterfactual: Increasing support, worsening perfusion or recurrent supra-systemic pressure would make further stabilization the priority.

choices.label: Continue stabilization before reconsidering the repair
choices.rationale: This fits ongoing instability, but intubation and residual sub-systemic pulmonary hypertension do not by themselves outweigh the current trajectory.
choices.temptation: Treat any pulmonary hypertension or ventilator use as prohibiting repair.
choices.residentError: Demand normalization rather than interpreting current readiness.
choices.decidingObservation: Perfusion and oxygenation are sustained while pulmonary pressure has fallen below systemic.
choices.counterfactual: Rising oxygen requirement, falling urine output, increasing lactate or supra-systemic pulmonary pressure would favor further stabilization.

choices.label: Assess ECMO escalation before planning the repair
choices.rationale: ECMO assessment is relevant to instability despite maximal support, which this record does not show.
choices.temptation: Interpret persistent thoracic bowel and pulmonary hypertension as failed conventional stabilization.
choices.residentError: Escalate from anatomy instead of the support/perfusion trajectory.
choices.decidingObservation: Oxygenation and perfusion are sustained on conventional support without inotropes.
choices.counterfactual: Refractory instability despite maximal medical support could warrant ECMO suitability assessment before deciding the repair sequence.

nodes.explanation: Persistent hernia and intubation do not themselves determine timing. Interpret the whole trend: perfusion and oxygenation have been sustained and estimated pulmonary pressure is now below systemic. The current CAHS guideline supports considering repair after physiological readiness is sustained, with the neonatal, surgical and anesthesia teams confirming the plan. This is not automatic operative clearance or a guarantee of safety; renewed instability would change the sequence.
reasoningSteps: Integrate sustained oxygenation and perfusion with the pressure trend, recognizing that 45 mmHg is below simultaneous systemic pressure of 70 mmHg despite residual pulmonary hypertension.
Select repair planning on continuing support rather than demanding normalization or escalating to ECMO without refractory instability.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Defer solely because intubation and residual pulmonary hypertension remain.
nodes.decidingObservation: For a day, oxygenation/perfusion measures have been reassuring and estimated pulmonary pressure has fallen below systemic.
nodes.counterfactual: Change the record to increasing oxygen support, falling urine output, rising lactate and supra-systemic pulmonary pressure: further stabilization before repair becomes the best plan. Refractory instability on maximal support would raise ECMO assessment.
nodes.deletionTest: The sustained interval, oxygen requirement, perfusion and simultaneous pressures contribute independently. Persistent radiographic hernia preserves the anatomy-versus-physiology tension. No operative route or invented immediate-repair deadline is scored.

authorGate.cueAttack: Three sequencing plans replace one stabilization option against two immediate operations. Raw values do not say ready or stable. Residual pulmonary hypertension and intubation preserve a credible deferral temptation.
authorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: Three perioperative sequencing plans for the outside tertiary team: repair on present support, more conventional stabilization, or ECMO assessment before repair.
authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Integrate sustained oxygenation and perfusion with the pressure trend, recognizing that 45 mmHg is below simultaneous systemic pressure of 70 mmHg despite residual pulmonary hypertension. Select repair planning on continuing support rather than demanding normalization or escalating to ECMO without refractory instability.
authorGate.predictedDifficulty: Moderate to hard author prediction: distinguish sub-systemic from normal pressure, integrate respiratory/perfusion evidence and avoid deferral solely because ICU support persists.
authorGate.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: The directly read May 2026 CAHS 15-page government guideline supports these readiness measures. Fictional FiO2 0.30 is below both published 0.4-0.5 bounds; no ambiguous threshold is tested. Independent older review supports stabilization before repair. No automatic timer, preferred route or ECMO eligibility cutoff invented.

manualGateForExactAfter.cueAttack: Removed treatment-being-arranged, duplicated inflammation and cancellation cues. Each choice is a definite operation with comparable timing language. Prior extent and current response are separate raw records.
manualGateForExactAfter.decisionStageAndCategory: Three definitive operative plans combining extent and timing; acute infection care is shared. This is not an airway-rescue or urgent drainage task.
manualGateForExactAfter.twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret persistent local inflammation despite fever improvement as an unresolved active episode. Use prior operative extent to retain definitive tract/hyoid surgery while placing it after infection resolution.
manualGateForExactAfter.predictedDifficulty: Moderate author prediction: systemic improvement tempts premature surgery, while the prior simple operation tempts another incomplete excision. No automatic hard label.
manualGateForExactAfter.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: The task explicitly concerns definitive surgery. Active local findings determine timing and prior retained tract/hyoid determines extent. Feedback preserves clinically indicated urgent drainage and supplies no exact waiting interval or medication rule.
manualGateForExactAfter.sequenceCheck: Standalone revision: no prior scored feedback. This v2 has not received independent PASS; no multipart case is admitted from author checks.

manualGateForExactAfter.cueAttack: The header gives a visit reason. All choices commit to treatment plans; surgery is not just a reasonable referral scored as wrong. Goals distinguish observation without substituting for the response and examination.
manualGateForExactAfter.decisionStageAndCategory: Three treatment commitments: renewed bracing, operative correction or observation. A referral for discussion is not equated with deciding to operate.
manualGateForExactAfter.twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret exposure-linked response and compressibility as mechanical responsiveness rather than an adequately demonstrated brace failure. Choose a renewed fitted course at the same treatment-commitment stage as surgery or observation, using willingness only to establish feasibility.
manualGateForExactAfter.predictedDifficulty: Fair moderate author prediction after repair. Actual exposure and response must be interpreted; removing the word failure does not establish hard difficulty.
manualGateForExactAfter.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: Compressibility, observed response and willingness support a fitted course. Surgical consultation remains reasonable; the scored competitor is operative commitment. Exact wear schedules, pressure thresholds and guaranteed outcomes remain withheld.
manualGateForExactAfter.sequenceCheck: Standalone revision: no prior scored feedback. This v2 has not received independent PASS; no multipart case is admitted from author checks.

manualGateForExactAfter.cueAttack: Raw exhibit avoids the parotid diagnostic label. Competitors are real exposures for other congenital neck routes, of comparable length and scope. No skin-only or total-gland extreme. Explicit nerve identification remains in the operative answer and teaching.
manualGateForExactAfter.decisionStageAndCategory: Three planned surgical exposures after mapping and infection resolution. Imaging acquisition and limited abscess treatment are not competing stages.
manualGateForExactAfter.twoConsequentialSteps: Infer the first-branchial/parotid route from cutaneous and ear-canal endpoints plus intervening salivary tissue. Choose an exposure permitting complete tract dissection with facial-nerve protection rather than an exposure for another branchial route.
manualGateForExactAfter.predictedDifficulty: Moderate author prediction: infer the less common ear-canal route before selecting its nerve-safe exposure, against a credible common second-branchial exposure.
manualGateForExactAfter.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: The endpoints distinguish the routes. Adams et al. supports the first-branchial operation and contrasting second/lower routes. One eligible anatomical source and variable nerve relation remain explicit limitations.
manualGateForExactAfter.sequenceCheck: Standalone revision: no prior scored feedback. This v2 has not received independent PASS; no multipart case is admitted from author checks.

manualGateForExactAfter.cueAttack: Three sequencing plans replace one stabilization option against two immediate operations. Raw values do not say ready or stable. Residual pulmonary hypertension and intubation preserve a credible deferral temptation.
manualGateForExactAfter.decisionStageAndCategory: Three perioperative sequencing plans for the outside tertiary team: repair on present support, more conventional stabilization, or ECMO assessment before repair.
manualGateForExactAfter.twoConsequentialSteps: Integrate sustained oxygenation and perfusion with the pressure trend, recognizing that 45 mmHg is below simultaneous systemic pressure of 70 mmHg despite residual pulmonary hypertension. Select repair planning on continuing support rather than demanding normalization or escalating to ECMO without refractory instability.
manualGateForExactAfter.predictedDifficulty: Moderate to hard author prediction: distinguish sub-systemic from normal pressure, integrate respiratory/perfusion evidence and avoid deferral solely because ICU support persists.
manualGateForExactAfter.oneDefensibleBestAnswer: The directly read May 2026 CAHS 15-page government guideline supports these readiness measures. Fictional FiO2 0.30 is below both published 0.4-0.5 bounds; no ambiguous threshold is tested. Independent older review supports stabilization before repair. No automatic timer, preferred route or ECMO eligibility cutoff invented.

independentPassRecord.title: Tailor fixation to operative findings
fairness: The learner must distinguish the indication for exploration from the diagnosis actually found, then apply the absence of testicular torsion/bell-clapper anatomy to the fixation decision. Routine bilateral fixation does not follow merely because exploration occurred.

Untwisted cord, absence of ischemic change, normal attachments and a torted appendage support closing without testicular fixation among these choices. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the exact consensus recommendation remains subject to clinical sign-off.
The torted appendage is a legitimate operative diagnosis for a different management question, not an illicit pre-answer diagnosis label. The normal attachment finding is decision-critical.

Part 2 follows a justified urgent exploration and introduces a different operative decision. It states that exploration has already occurred and supplies its findings, so it stands alone without recalling the prior answer. Part 1 feedback does not teach fixation.

The initial high/horizontal lie and subsequent alternative operative diagnosis deserve clinician plausibility review as a complete case, but are not sufficient evidence of a definite contradiction or clinical error.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between torted appendage and torted testis, plus the attachment findings; without these the fixation comparison loses fairness.
For clearer post-answer attribution, identify the referenced consensus by name instead of saying only "this consensus". This is a feedback clarification, not a blocker to the scored decision.

answerChoices.label: Close without testicular fixation
answerChoices.rationale: FIX-IT consensus does not recommend routine fixation for an alternate pathology with neither testicular torsion nor bell-clapper anatomy.

answerChoices.rationale: The bilateral fixation rule for confirmed testicular torsion is not the rule for this negative exploration with normal anatomy.

independentPassRecord.title: Act on nonrepresentative node sampling
fairness: Excisional biopsy is the best of the listed plans for a progressively enlarging fixed cervical node after a sample containing no lymphoid tissue. The learner must reject the family-level reassurance as nonrepresentative sampling and integrate the continuing concerning examination.

Repeat FNA is a credible tempting response to a missed target, but does not offer the same definitive representative tissue/architecture as excision in this pediatric presentation. Surveillance is not supported by the progressive findings.
The necessary negative, "no lymphoid tissue is represented", is an actual adequacy finding rather than an unfair giveaway; removing it would change the inference.
No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical wording shortcut identified. The standalone presentation, current update and complete task cohere.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between a nondiagnostic specimen and a benign node. Keep the progressive examination findings and avoid adding a diagnosis label before answering.
Clinical sign-off should retain the pediatric context when confirming the ranking of excision versus repeat needle sampling; do not generalize this exact ranking to every neck mass.

independentPassRecord.title: Escalate persistent suppuration after medical treatment
fairness: The learner must separate systemic improvement from local treatment failure, then recognize that a progressing fluctuant fluid/debris collection needs drainage assessment. Continuing IV treatment can tempt a learner who overweights defervescence.

Surgical incision-and-drainage assessment is the best listed plan. Elective whole-node excision after recovery does not address the active suppurative problem. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The description of fluid/debris is sufficient for this management decision and does not promise an absent image. The repeated systemic/local response in update and exhibit is mildly redundant but does not make the question ambiguous.
The hospital decision time is explicit and the node stands alone. The explanation contrasts an indolent process after answering without depending on the separate Mina case.
suggestions: Retain both the improving systemic observations and worsening focal observations; the discordance supplies the consequential inference.
Optional tightening: remove the duplicate response sentence from either update or exhibit. Keep specialist assessment language from implying a procedure is automatically performed in the clinic.
